sourceInformation.source: Eye of the Beholder (Westwood Associates / SSI, 1991; MS-DOS and Amiga)
sourceInformation.genre: Real-time, first-person, grid-based party RPG dungeon crawler
sourceInformation.perspective: First-person party view on a grid with tweened steps and quarter turns, plus a top-down automap
sourceInformation.tech: my-3D2dge v0.85.2 (2D engine from dist/handoff) and my-3D2dge 3D v0.85.2 (three.js r182 WebGPU / WebGL 2, Rapier 0.19.3, via jsDelivr); AI Hub session client 1.4.0; Node 24 and Playwright 1.63.0 for the tests; plain JavaScript in one HTML file.
sourceInformation.artDirection: The engine's native retro-modern look: code-drawn low-res 3D (pixel resolution, toon light, outlines, fog), rigs as pixel-art cards, procedural textures, pen-drawn mechanisms and boss, a brass "lockwork" UI.
sourceInformation.animation: The engine's procedural rigs and moves (E.Humanoid, E.Blob), a tweened first-person camera, pen-animated mechanisms and the Bolt-Holder, telegraphed monster wind-ups and first-person weapon swings.
sourceInformation.audio: The engine's chip synth (step-sequencer songs with a combat layer, stings, synthesized sfx). Voices from a custom WebAudio formant babble synth (Animalese/Simlish style). No audio files.
sourceInformation.online: AI Hub Session Protocol v1, ghost mode, 1 to 4 players (the Rat Run race); a solo time trial against your own best-run ghost.
sourceInformation.testing: Headless: Node vm tests of the sim, content lint, a scripted playthrough bot, and Playwright (Chromium, WebGL 2) browser checks plus the AI Hub harness. Screenshots only for what scripts cannot judge. No subagents.
sourceInformation.research: Planning research from PLAN.md (Giant Bomb, MobyGames, oldgames.sk and knowledge of the source); engine docs and the crawler kit read in the build.
sourceInformation.environment: Claude Code CLI (headless); Linux; browser unknown (tested in headless Chromium).

testingFeedback: About 15. The main ones: the engine header's "</script>" text broke the inlined bundle; the 5x7 font lacks several symbols (dashes, blocks, check marks); a world only has a fixed number of lights, so making them on every floor entry ran out; top-level names clashing in the single module; the bot treated monsters behind a gate as threats and froze; picking up or stowing while facing a door opened the door instead; a non-modal dialogue froze game time in the attract mode; a spinner cell blocked the bot's pathing; an item dropped in a doorway was never collected; hub progress reports were tied to game time (slow in a software renderer); and three balance problems (a level 1 party wiped by the first den, XP too slow, a boss the scripted party could not beat).
Six: the broken bundle, the light exhaustion on re-entering a floor, the module-order boot crash, the attract mode freezing in its second scene, the first-den wipe and the unwinnable boss.

The scripted full playthrough: a bot that plays by the real rules through the same commands as a player, from New Game to the ending. It found the pacing, soft-lock and balance faults that unit checks could not, and it doubles as the attract mode and Dev Mode auto-play. Running the browser checks with game.advance() (no rendering) was a close second.

Wall-clock screenshot and attract-mode waits in headless Chromium. The software renderer runs at about 4 fps (0.2x game speed), so the waits were slow and told me little until I switched to game.advance().
engineFeedback: That one small API gives a whole game: fixed 1/120 s steps with game.advance for tests, scenes, input with glyph labels and rebinding, settings, saves, a pause menu, Dialog, a chip synth, and a 3D world with pen-drawn things and rigs shown as pixel-art cards. Everything drawn by code made one HTML file with no assets easy.

Yes, a few times. The 3D engine header contains </script> text, which breaks an inline script. A world's lights must all be made at build time. The 5x7 font has a small character set. I guessed the Esc key would reach my cancel action, but the engine takes it for pause. World3D.init prints a deprecation note for its parameters.

The whole party-RPG layer: a pure deterministic sim (grid movement, wiring language, plates, locks, pits, teleporters, secrets, real-time cooldown combat with telegraphed monsters, magic slots, camp, hunger, XP, boss), a presenter that mirrors it into the 3D world, a focus-based 10-foot UI kit, the babble voice synth, and the walkthrough bot.

Making the first-person grid crawler fit it: the engine thinks in free-moving bodies, so movement, doors and collision are in my sim and the 3D hero is only a camera anchor. Making secret and illusory walls look like the baked walls was also fiddly. A software renderer made visual checks slow.

Two small patches: the Button symbols setting now defaults to PlayStation and offers only PlayStation and Xbox; and audio gained bus(name) with a voice bus and sfx(name, { pan }) through a stereo panner. Dwarf beards are drawn by the game over portraits, not patched into E.Humanoid.

Ship a grid-crawler helper in the 3D engine: cell-based movement and tween, wall features on a wall face, and doors and secret walls that reuse the level's wall material. I would also widen the pixel font's character set.
promptFeedback: It gave a clear target (a first-person party crawler), a complete order of work, the exact tests and the hub rules. The plan's data tables made it quick to build the content.

The plan asks for more than a medium-effort session can build: four floors plus a race, 18 spells, 16 monsters, pen-drawn creatures, a Veil branch and several engine patches. It was not always clear which parts could be cut, and the "cut quantity, never a system" rule conflicts with that scale.

Scoping the plan down to a vertical slice that still has every system (attract mode, Dev Mode, 10-foot UI, hub ghost race, a bot full playthrough) and keeping it balanced, while the only renderer available is slow.

Add a ranked list of must-haves and cuts for each effort level, and give one full reference floor with its walkthrough data. State what a pass looks like for the hub harness on a slow machine. Allow engine features such as a voice bus to be optional.

aiHub.name: Eye of the Bolt-Holder
aiHub.description: A real-time, first-person party dungeon crawl beneath Hasp, the City of a Thousand Locks: four floors of drains, clockwork halls and eye-cults, levers, plates and keys, spells memorized at camp, and the caged Eye that holds the city's bolts. Race the Rat Run against up to three other parties.
aiHub.controls: Stick/WASD move · D-pad/Q E turn · ✕/F use · □/Space strike · L2 R2/1-6 hands · △/I party
